solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What prisoners need starting sentence

parts.note: the word prisoners, placed first in a sentence, must begin with an upper-case letter at its head

explanation.surface: Inmates seem to need something before their jail term can begin.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests jailbirds awaiting a court term; really it is about writing the word 'prisoners' at the start of a sentence, where its first letter must be upper case.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentence-initial word takes an upper-case initial, so the word for inmates needs its first letter enlarged.

clue.text: Chancellor's fortune

indicators.note: the apostrophe s stands for has: the first word has the letters inside it

explanation.surface: A Treasury minister's personal wealth is under discussion.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortune in the sense of luck or fate is a synonym of happenstance or lot.

clue.text: Large number in favour of union

parts.note: pro is Latin-derived for for, in favour of
fusion is a joining or union of things

explanation.surface: A large crowd backs the idea of a merger.
explanation.definitionFit: An abundance or great quantity is a lavish plentiful supply, a large number of things.

clue.text: Reduce expenses — and the waistline, simultaneously!

definitions.text: Reduce expenses — and the waistline, simultaneously!

parts.words: Reduce expenses — and the waistline, simultaneously!
parts.note: the idiom for economising literally describes pulling a strap tighter round a slimmer middle

explanation.surface: Cutting back on spending also trims the figure, the clue jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for cutting spending is read literally too: pulling the strap round your middle in a notch.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to economise, and taken literally it describes cinching a strap round a thinner middle.

clue.text: Want stupid yes-men who bow and scrape?

parts.note: to want is to lack, be without

indicators.note: stupid suggests the letters of yes are muddled into a silly order

explanation.surface: A question whether one wants foolish sycophants who grovel.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'yes-men' looks like one word, but splits into the fodder for 'stupid' and the start of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Servile followers or flunkeys are people who fawn on their masters, bowing and scraping.

clue.text: Loud instruments? Hardly!

parts.note: f, forte, is the musical marking for loud
lutes are stringed instruments

explanation.surface: A wry aside that these woodwinds are hardly noisy.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as wordplay, 'Loud instruments' is F plus LUTES; the whole clue also describes the answer, whose soft sound means it is hardly loud.
explanation.definitionFit: Gentle woodwinds are instruments seldom thought of as loud, which the clue's exclamation remarks on.

clue.text: Doesn't interfere at all, so remains thirsty, maybe

definitions.meaning: to refrain from meddling with something that is fine as it is
read literally, someone who will not touch the water source stays without a drink

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps out of things ends up going without a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means not to meddle; literally, ignoring the water source leaves one parched.

clue.text: One has a crack in this German city

definitions.meaning: someone who has a go or makes an attempt
a city on the Moselle in western Germany

explanation.surface: Someone goes for it in a city in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a crack means attempting; someone who attempts is one who tries, and the word also names a Moselle city.

clue.text: It is kept in stable to disinfect

indicators.note: kept in says the first words are held inside the word for stable

parts.note: mentally stable is sane
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is kept in a stable so the stall can be cleaned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stable' looks like a horse's stall, but here means mentally balanced.
explanation.definitionFit: To disinfect is to make hygienic, cleansing of germs.

clue.text: Cat returns to me with a dog's dinner

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: returns says the word for cat comes back, read in reverse

parts.note: puss is a familiar word for a cat

explanation.surface: A cat comes back to its owner, along with the dog's food.
explanation.walkthrough: A dog's dinner is British slang for a muddle or botch; the cat's name is turned round and attached after the clue's own pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's dinner is British slang for a muddle, which is what a botched job or a shambles is.

clue.text: A pine showing lengthwise

parts.note: to pine for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: A pine tree is displayed lying lengthways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pine' looks like the tree, but is the verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: Lengthwise means in the direction of the length, from end to end.

clue.text: Asian race resettled in tricky operation

indicators.note: resettled suggests the letters are moved to new positions

explanation.surface: An Asian people moving home is a delicate business.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgical delivery of a baby through the abdomen is a well-known, delicate operation.

clue.text: Legion left in protection of noble lady

indicators.note: in protection of says the short piece is sheltered inside the longer one

parts.note: a countess is a noblewoman, an earl's wife

explanation.surface: A Roman legion leaves a noblewoman under guard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legion' looks like a body of soldiers, but is the adjective meaning innumerable.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective, legion means very numerous, beyond counting.

clue.text: Deplore losing river bird

indicators.note: losing says a letter is dropped from the word for deplore

parts.note: to deplore is to regret

explanation.surface: Someone laments the loss of a waterbird from the river.
explanation.definitionFit: The heron-like wading bird with white plumage is a kind of bird.

clue.text: Fanatics found among Quakers, mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all of the word for Quakers is kept

parts.note: Quakers are the Religious Society of Friends

explanation.surface: Zealots turn up among a Quaker meeting, for the most part.
explanation.walkthrough: Quakers are formally the Society of Friends; 'mostly' takes one letter, the R, out of FRIENDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiend is informal for an enthusiast or addict, as in a fitness fiend, so fanatics.

clue.text: Exotic fruit looks like animal's foot (feet)

parts.note: a paw is the foot of an animal
paws in the plural are animal feet

explanation.surface: A tropical fruit is said to resemble an animal's foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The papaya, a tropical fruit, is also known by a reduplicated name.

clue.text: Their act, bizarrely, needs conservative designer

indicators.note: bizarrely says the letters are thrown into a strange order

explanation.surface: A strange stage routine requires a cautious planner.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviation for conservative goes into the pool before 'bizarrely' rearranges it, since neither half of the answer can be built without it.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who designs buildings is the professional designer of houses and offices.

clue.text: Get wrong girl, say, to act as umpire

indicators.note: say signals the word for girl is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: Miss is a title for a girl or unmarried woman
to judge is to act as an umpire or referee

explanation.surface: A young woman mistakenly gets asked to referee a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' means the girl's title only sounds right; the double S of MISS is written as one.
explanation.definitionFit: To misjudge is to assess wrongly, form a mistaken opinion of.

clue.text: Limitless prize money cricketers must have

indicators.note: limitless here means the word loses its leading edge

parts.note: winnings are money won as a prize

explanation.surface: Unlimited prize money is something cricketers insist on.
explanation.walkthrough: An innings is a team's or batter's turn at batting in cricket, something every cricketing side must have.
explanation.definitionFit: Each cricket side needs a turn at batting, its spell at the crease.

clue.text: Alternate witness, present and past

parts.note: to witness is to see; in the present tense he sees
the past tense of see is saw

explanation.surface: A substitute witness gives testimony about now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alternate' looks like a substitute but is the verb: to go up and down by turns.
explanation.definitionFit: To move up and down or back and forth by turns is to alternate, like a playground plank.

clue.text: Plan to replace yen with euros, primarily, becomes the law

indicators.note: to replace says a letter in the word for plan is taken out and swapped
with names the letter that goes in where the old one came out

parts.note: a policy is a plan of action
Y is the usual abbreviation for the Japanese yen

indicators.note: primarily picks the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A scheme to swap the yen for the euro becomes legally binding.
explanation.definitionFit: The law is informal for the officers who enforce it, the constabulary.

clue.text: Saw dog get tangled in lead

indicators.note: get tangled in says the dog ends up caught inside the lead

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
Rover is a traditional name for a dog

explanation.surface: A dog seen getting caught up in its lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a verb of seeing, but is a noun: an old saying. 'lead' is the metal, not a leash.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying or maxim, the same as an adage.

clue.text: Instrument of Death

parts.note: the Grim Reaper, personified Death, carries a long curved blade as his emblem

explanation.surface: A grim reference to a murder weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: Death personified, the Grim Reaper, is pictured carrying a long curved blade for cutting grass.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-bladed mowing tool is the emblem carried by the Grim Reaper.

clue.text: A Frenchman's work units, nothing less

indicators.note: less says something is taken away from the units of work

parts.note: joules are units of work or energy
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A French chap's work is measured in physical units.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules is a common French man's first name, as in Verne.

clue.text: Unusual roles one plays without success

indicators.note: unusual suggests the letters are put in an out-of-the-ordinary order

explanation.surface: An actor in odd parts never quite makes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fails to win, a player without success, is a failure in the game.

clue.text: I am my favourite subject, pathologically so

definitions.text: I am my favourite subject, pathologically so

parts.words: I am my favourite subject, pathologically so
parts.note: a person obsessively absorbed in themselves would say they are their own favourite topic

explanation.surface: Someone confesses an unhealthy fixation on talking about themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A person morbidly self-obsessed, whose own self is the favourite topic, is a narcissist.

clue.text: Wrong speed measure could be critical

indicators.note: wrong suggests the letters are set out in an incorrect order

parts.note: a rate is a measure, as of speed

explanation.surface: Getting a speed reading wrong could be serious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' turns SPEED into DESPE, followed by RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A critical situation is one so grave it is dire and urgent.

clue.text: Lover tries to show what's obvious

indicators.note: to show says the letters are on display within the first words

explanation.surface: A suitor makes efforts to show how plain his feelings are.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done openly, plain to see, is obvious rather than hidden.

clue.text: Mistakes made by a sailor about to retire

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the whole string is read in reverse

parts.note: a tar is a sailor
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Errors committed by a seaman on the point of retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: A, TAR and RE together make ATARRE; 'to retire' reverses the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata are a list of printing errors, the Latin plural for mistakes.

clue.text: Pupil who doesn't appear to be educated

definitions.text: Pupil who doesn't appear to be educated

parts.words: Pupil who doesn't appear to be educated
parts.note: a student who fails to turn up for lessons, rather than one who looks uneducated

explanation.surface: A student seems not to have been schooled at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't appear to be educated' looks like a judgement on learning, but means the pupil fails to show up for school.
explanation.definitionFit: A person missing from school or work, failing to attend, is one who is away.
